## Astra Chemistry — A stronger benchmark changes the research target

A significant correction emerged from the literature review: autonomous, DNA-programmed formation of non-DNA polymers has already been demonstrated.

Meng and colleagues published An autonomous molecular assembler for programmable chemical synthesis in Nature Chemistry in 2016. Their DNA machinery autonomously produced oligomers with programmed olefin or peptide bonds and recorded the synthesis sequence in DNA. An earlier DNA walker demonstrated autonomous multistep amine acylation in a shared solution. 

[image](https://www.google.com/s2/favicons?domain=https://www.nature.com\&sz=32)

Nature Chemistry

+1



Astra therefore cannot claim novelty merely by making a DNA-directed chemical assembler, a moving molecular instruction, or an autonomous sequence of peptide-forming reactions.

The distinctive unresolved capability is narrower and more demanding:

Multiple independently programmed products should advance only after the required permanent bond forms, remain at their current instruction after a harmless missed reaction, and continue correctly under common reagents without requiring individual observation.

The existing delayed-contact NCL construction remains a candidate, but it must outperform these established mechanisms on that exact capability—not just produce another programmed oligomer.

### New result: slow chemical intermediates can defeat an otherwise reliable instruction gate

The 2016 assembler paper identifies precisely the failure Astra is trying to overcome: its DNA machinery can progress before the intended covalent reaction finishes. The authors observed truncated products and identified premature DNA progression or reagent degradation as possible causes. Their mechanism did not require the DNA step to wait for the corresponding bond. 

[image](https://www.google.com/s2/favicons?domain=https://users.ox.ac.uk\&sz=32)

## Astra Chemistry — A missing failure pathway in the current relay

I reproduced the previous six-anchor reaction-and-wash model, including its reported 96.35% conditional completion probability for 1,024 additions with 5% displacement spillover.

The next attack identifies a potentially important omission: the model allows an unreacted donor to remain chemically active during washing, but does not allow that donor to form a new irreversible wrong bond during that interval.

This matters because native chemical ligation is not stopped merely by beginning a wash. Reactive peptide thioesters can continue participating in exchange reactions, including reactions involving internal cysteine residues. A 2025 study of NCL catalysts explicitly identifies branched thioesters on internal cysteines as competing products and investigates their reversal. 

[image](https://www.google.com/s2/favicons?domain=https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov\&sz=32)

PMC



Thus donor disappearance and chemical harmlessness are separate properties. The existing 96.35% result is valid for its stated model but cannot be interpreted as the fidelity of an integrated peptide assembler unless reactions occurring during donor clearance are also charged.

### Exact result: how much incorrect chemistry can occur during donor clearance?

I added irreversible wrong-bond transitions to the existing chemical-and-anchor reaction network. The extended model retains the same retry dynamics and actual anchor-docking states; it does not reset stalled molecules to a favourable configuration.

## Astra Chemistry — A more consequential constraint on pre-commit proofreading

The previous model treated each proofreading round as an irreversible rejection of incorrect donors. That assumption needs to be made physical.

Mukherjee and colleagues' 2024 DNA proofreading system uses a fuel-driven pathway that converts rejected monomers into waste while returning the template to a usable state. It is not merely a reversible DNA binding-and-unbinding cycle. 

[image](https://www.google.com/s2/favicons?domain=https://pubs.acs.org\&sz=32)

ACS Publications



This distinction is essential for Astra.

If a rejected wrong donor remains chemically competent and can repeatedly rebind, rejection may only delay its eventual incorporation. In a finite-state system with a nonzero chance of reaching the reactive state on each attempt, indefinitely repeated attempts eventually reach that state with probability one, unless the donor can be irreversibly removed, neutralized or destroyed first.

The leading mechanism therefore needs a physical wrong-donor sink, not only improved DNA recognition.

There is a useful chemical starting point: CAPTN demonstrated selective activation of latent peptide-thioester precursors. In particular, its Nbz and hydrazide precursor strategies permit different peptide segments to be activated in stages. But CAPTN required controlled reagent and pH changes, and did not demonstrate fuel-driven selective activation of different donors sharing one bath. 

[image](https://www.google.com/s2/favicons?domain=https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov\&sz=32)

PMC



The unresolved construction becomes more specific: can DNA proofreading irreversibly reject the wrong peptide donor while leaving the rooted parent competent, and can the retained correct donor subsequently be activated without also activating the rejected material?
